Name: -1_manor_place_maiden_door
Representative_Docs:
["Oh, we poor manor spirits  
Other poor laborers  
Ordinary third ones  
Helper spirits fourth  
Drinkers fifth  
Were driven to howl at night  
To march across the land  
To walk across the desert.  
Night is painful, moon is painful  
God’s fire is painful  
Night is painful, I cut the hay  
Moon is painful, I cut the stack  
God’s fire is painful,  
Golden rakes in the shed  
Silver sickle handles  
When will I escape the manor's year?  
The manor’s year is a hellish year.  
I escape as if from under your mouth  
Between the jaws of a lion.  
Between the teeth of a monkey  
Now I look back carefully  
On my dog’s load I turn my head.  
Before the home gate  
Before father’s barn door,  
Before brother’s chamber threshold  
Then I look over the ridge  
Towards the worse side,  
See how the hell looks  
The underworlds blaze  
Hell’s windows glow red  
Ghost towers stand idle  
Life seems a joke.  
There are large German fields  
Bottomless lady’s fields.  
There our feathers melt  
Silver ornaments straighten out.  
Wallets grow empty.  
There on the big field  
On the bottomless field.  
On the angular meadow.  
Now I say again in reverse.  
To sing again in Danish  
I turn the words upside down.  
There fall on the back of the German  
Break the mistress’s neck  
Lady’s hip bones fall apart  
Virgin’s limbs twist  
Our backs become whole  
Our scythes sharp  
Our necks stiff.", 'Moon, moon, little gold
Fern, fern, little leaf
Where was the little gold?
Gold like a haystack
Where was the gold’s little head?
Like a manor measure box
Where were the gold’s little eyes?
Like silver beads
Where were the gold’s little ears?
Like a piece of gold leaf
Where was the gold’s little feather?
A feather from a smoky fur
Where was the gold’s little beak?
Like a bit of wind
Where were the gold’s little feet?
Feet like a hare’s feet
Where were the gold’s little claws?
Like the village ploughshares,
The servant boys’ hardworking ploughshares
Oh, you crazy little gold
You’re looking for the honeycomb
You are looking under the honeycomb’s shadow
We have a chicken on the threshing floor,
The rooster’s golden cellar,
Two chickens in the flock,
Three door keepers,
Four link carriers,
Five key holders,
Six on the locks.
Go to that farm
Where there is a chicken on the threshing floor,
On the dry straw of the rooster.
“Hello, hello man, what are you doing here?”
“I am digging a hole.”
“What will you do with that hole?”
“I will draw in charcoal.”
“What will you do with that charcoal?”
“I will put a pot on it.”
“What will you do with that pot?”
“I will put water in it.”
“What will you do with that water?”
“I will take the feathers of the hen and the rooster.”
“What wrong did the hen and the rooster do?”
“The lord’s trench was plowed,
and the maiden took the peas away.”
“Where were you earlier?”
“Down the hill I built a fence.”
“Where were the women and children?”
“They were carrying wood and reeds.”
“How long was the fence?”
“As high as the sky.
How wide?
As wide as the blade of an axe.
How thick?
Like a sieve for oats.”', "Three on the daughter's knee  
The first was Ella’s knee  
That was Ella grandmother’s knee  
The middle one was dear husband’s knee  
That was dear husband’s knee  
The last was the wretched knee  
That was evil husband’s knee  
Sudden father-in-law’s knee  
Sudden mother-in-law’s knee  
Künastu servant’s knee  
Nurjatu midwife’s knee  
The mad man’s knee  
When it was Ella grandmother’s knee  
Then you could run around in a shirt  
You could flutter in linen  
When it was dear husband’s knee  
The middle one was dear husband’s knee  
That was dear husband’s knee  
You could eat in the shed  
Secretly you could eat in the sauna  
Surely you could eat in the kitchen too  
In the double-layered blanket  
Even more in the living room  
Finally, that was evil husband’s knee  
Sudden father-in-law’s knee  
Sudden servant’s knee  
Nurjatu midwife’s knee  
The mad man’s knee  
You could cry in the shed  
You could cry in the sauna  
Surely you could cry in the kitchen too  
In the double-layered blanket  
Even more in the living room  
Everything comes upon  
The pig’s eye falls upon  
Father-in-law came upon, mother-in-law came upon  
Father-in-law came with a bull’s yoke  
Mother-in-law came with a cow-milker  
The midwife on the stove porch roof  
Her husband was a stone fist  
I got from the door to the yard  
Through the gate I got out  
Then I got more on the back  
I didn’t wait, I came out  
I went back quickly  
Then I go back inside  
I throw the chips on the bench  
Already the father-in-law spoke of goodness  
Already the mother-in-law spoke of goodness  
The servant spoke of gold  
Her husband had gone astray  
Already I was at home  
Who went from the door to the yard  
Went out through the gate  
Then began to argue back  
Began to scold the father-in-law  
To speak against misfortune  
To beg my husband  
Be well father-in-law  
Be well mother-in-law  
Teach the son goodness  
Don’t put him to sleep on the patch  
Don’t send him to the stove  
Forced to do heavier work  
Commanded to work faster  
Don’t put him to drink vodka  
Don’t make him want sour wine  
Don’t make him taste bitter beer  
Teach him to drink beer  
Wait, wait, come on, mother-in-law  
Let him go to the tavern a second time  
I dig a hole under the door  
Put chains on the hole  
I throw branches on the floor  
When he comes home from the tavern  
He immediately steps into the hole  
Breaks his neck on the branches."]

Name: 0_manor_hay_young maiden_grandmother
Representative_Docs:
["I heard the village rocking,  
the village whispering,  
I took to my tasks,  
I began to move step by step:  
I carried hay to the mountain,  
into the cellar under the door,  
I opened the lid of the chest,  
the lid of the painted chest;  
I took the whitest from the chest,  
I took the axe from the chest,  
eagerly mounted on my back  
a slender, pointed spear,  
a bucket of water,  
linen stockings up to the toes.  
Overhead came a big night,  
as if a rainy rainbow,  
around it spread a big cloak,  
as if half a reindeer skin.  
I laid out the wide apron,  
as if new barn doors.  
On my chest, I placed a big brooch,  
as if the moon in the sky.  
On my neck, a grandmother’s barley straw,  
like a hen laying straw eggs.  
On my head, I put a big wreath,  
like a large rooster's comb.  
On my finger, I linked a ring,  
like stars in the sky.  
On my foot, I wore woolen socks,  
at the end, shoes tied with straps,  
then I went rocking to the village,  
whispering through the village.  
There they moved boldly around,  
the district was full of mischief,  
bread was gold-like fine,  
I laid my apron on the floor,  
mist swirled over the fir trees.", 'Hello, hello, little family  
Hello new doors of the family  
Hello birches of the market  
Hello branches of the island  
Lift the latch, Leenokene  
Open the door, Annekene  
Mari, get the ribbons ready  
Are you maidens going home?  
Mistress, little maiden  
Let the vagabond Mardis in  
Take the shoes from the room  
Stockings from the big edge  
Step into the barn  
Hurry to the cellar  
Look for a share for Mardi  
Try to get fish for Mardi  
Bring a piece of raw meat  
A plate of white beans  
Two or three pancakes  
Five or six sausage pieces  
The family grandmother is an old lady  
What I promise you  
Fill the doorways with grain  
Threshing floors  
Fill the sheep’s barn  
Flood the pigsty with straw  
Fill the manure pits  
Master, little master  
What I promise you  
Horse stable, braiding sheds  
Close walls fattening  
The hay must be good  
House girl, little maiden  
May six suitors come to her  
Some go, others come  
The third must stay at home  
Servant, little servant  
What I promise you  
Iron gun, forest signal  
Drooping ears of the little dog  
May your pigs die  
Piglets fall ill with cough  
Gray bulls fail.', 'Oh, dear Väetsa village  
Where birch trees grew in curls  
Grandmother’s daughters are beautiful  
Father’s daughters are calm  
Grandma’s daughters are cheerful  
The boy’s daughter is crying  
The girl is crying for her husband  
The madman shouts for the groom  
I am crying for grandma’s daughter  
I pity the plowmen  
The pure porridge cookers  
The clear blacksmiths -  
Mother was taken from the door  
Lovers left through the window  
Mother was taken along the road  
Lovers went through the gardens  
Mother was laid in the grave  
Lovers went down the hill  
We, two orphans  
Go to the John’s Day church  
Black scarves in hand  
We go to mother’s grave  
One wipes the other’s eyes  
One kisses the other’s neck  
One strokes the other’s head -  
Rise up, dear mother  
Rise up to groom my head  
To prepare the gift box  
To fix the coffin lid -  
You cannot rise, daughter, no  
You cannot rise, no use  
Never before has it been so  
That a schoolteacher is at home  
Give the village to the plowman  
May God comb your head  
The Creator grant you mercy  
Mary protect you in heaven -  
Rise up, dear mother -  
You cannot rise, no use  
Grass had grown over the earth  
Hay over the grave  
Cowslips over the brow  
Alder tree catkins over the ears -  
Rise up, dear mother  
I bring a sand sieve from the town  
From the borough I bring a sieve  
I sift that coarse sand  
I knead that rough soil -  
I feed grass to the calves  
Hay to the oxen  
Bluebells to the cows  
Cowslips to the roosters  
Henbane to the hens. -']

Name: 2_beers_beer_drank_drink
Representative_Docs:
['At Umalas, the mountain owl calls,  
The pine cone rattles down the shore:  
"Come home, young man,  
Take me in a sack to your home."  
Place me on the edge of the board,  
From there I roll into the cluster,  
I crawl into the half-glass of beer,  
I slip between the branches."  
From there, beer reaches the cheek,  
Joy of the strong four-armed.  
I take senses from the heads of men,  
Half the senses from the heads of boys,  
Thanks to the wise women's heads.  
Men make noise without hats,  
Women dance without skirts,  
Girls run without belts,  
Boys with half boots.', "Hops called me into the ditch,  
Cone creaked into the corner stove  
Come here, young men,  
Take me to the hut of the bear,  
Make me a steed for the stag,  
Put me to dry on the railing.  
From there I go to the barn,  
Slip into the half-pint of beer,  
Roll between the twigs;  
Then I take the senses from men's heads,  
Half the senses from boys' heads,  
Thanks from wise women's heads;  
Men roar without hats,  
Women dance without the ground,  
Boys half without boots,  
Girls without belts.", "In the hollow, a pine cone calls into the stream  
A cone crackles into the bush  
In the grassy rye field  
Come here, young men  
Take me to the sack at home  
Set me on the bench by the stove  
Put me on the board to dry  
From there I roll into the cellar  
But I slip into the half-beer glass  
Drift into the beer mug  
Sink into the beer anchor  
Make me a good beer  
That takes away men's senses  
Half of the senses from the boys' heads  
Thanks to wise women's heads  
Men grumble without hats  
Women dance without cloth  
Girls without belts  
Boys with crooked backs  
One drinks from one hand to the other  
Mothers-in-law, mothers with buckets  
Look, I drink from the pail  
I feed my head through the pipe  
Do I drink from the cupboard, or from the jug  
Or do I drink from the colorful cup  
The cone makes the eyes colorful  
The jug makes the neck stiff."]

A patch of bog at the edge

And it were up to me to act,

The ladies into sticks,

Name: 4_riga_mistress_wreath_maidens
Representative_Docs:
['Oh, our golden king!  
Rich young gentleman of Riga,  
A true boy from Pärnu.  
Why didn’t you come to us last year,  
When the rivers ran without oil,  
And the springs bubbled below;  
When the surface swirled in whirlpools,  
Now you have come at the beginning of time,  
At the light springtime;  
At the rustling autumn,  
At the snowy snowfall of winter.  
Now you strip off your clothes:  
Rip off your collars,  
Take off your wreath from your head!  
Oh, our golden king!  
Rich young gentleman of Riga,  
A true boy from Pärnu,  
Give me some poor gold;  
Cast away the troublesome silver!  
Last year the master bought a press.  
The mistress got a little burden;  
I myself got a shawl’s worth;  
The press I got from beating the thigh,  
The broth I got from boiling the soup,  
From kneading the bread with a clasp.', 'Oh king, little king,  
Rich Saxon of Riga.  
Why didn’t you come to us last year?  
When the rivers ran without oil,  
When the old men brewed vodka.  
We brewed kvass in the cellars,  
Beat the ashes for firewood,  
Cleared the streets of mud,  
The village smelled of cumin,  
The village pastures of sulfur,  
Now you come to the white time,  
Now you come to the sad month,  
To the light spring,  
To the noisy autumn,  
To the winter snowfall.  
Now you strip off clothes,  
Break neck chains,  
Large brooches from the chest,  
Golden necklaces from the neck,  
Save the wreath from the head.  
Oh king, little king,  
Rich Saxon of Riga,  
Give me back poor gold,  
Poor gold, poor copper,  
Neither were these your shares,  
Nor were these your precious gifts,  
Nor was a fine feast brought,  
These I earned myself.  
I got the brooch from kneading bread,  
The necklace from boiling broth,  
The belt from beating the brachet,  
I bought myself a dwelling.  
Oh king, little king,  
Rich Saxon of Riga,  
What shall I offer you?  
I have one ox for plowing,  
One horse for raking,  
One cow for milking,  
One sheep in the barn,  
One pig in the sty,  
One hen on the roof,  
What shall I offer you?  
The ox I have for plowing the field,  
The horse for harrowing,  
The cow for milking the family,  
The sheep for shading the family,  
The pig for feeding the family,  
The rooster for crowing in the morning,  
The dog was outside barking.', 'O, our golden king!  
Rich gentleman of Riga,  
True boy of Pärnu.  
Why didn’t you come to us last year  
When the rivers ran without oil?  
You stirred from the deep spring,  
You twisted from the shallow pond,  
Now you have come at just the right time!  
At the light spring,  
At the dry autumn,  
At the snowy winter,  
Now you tear off your clothes,  
Break off your neck chains,  
Take the wreath from your head!  
“O, our golden king!  
Rich gentleman of Riga,  
True boy of Pärnu,  
Give me poor gold;  
Throw away the troublesome silver.  
My master bought a press:  
My mistress the prong,  
I myself got a bit of shawl,  
Got a press from making leg ribbons,  
Got some broth from cooking soup,  
A buckle from kneading bread.”']

Name: 6_little bird_sing_shouts_bird

['The cuckoo falls into the spruce forest,

Cuckoo’s sons in the lap,  
Cuckoo’s daughters in the hand.  
The cuckoo to my prayer:  
The family daughter, a young maiden,  
Give my sons to the hand!  
Tomorrow I will go to a new town  
Buy new leather shoes  
I will lace them with silk ribbons  
On top, red ribbons  
Underneath, beautiful anklets.  
Let me say again:  
The cuckoo does not fall to me,  
The cuckoo falls to the herdsman,  
Brightens the haymaker,  
Traps the hunter,

Rise up to become sprats  
Multiply into smelts  
Descend into burbots
